title: That they may all be one (John 17:20–26)
hookLine: he prays for all who will believe, that they may be one
last: IN THE WORLD, BUT NOT OF IT.

cards: Up to now, Jesus has been praying for the people at the table. Eleven men, tired and confused, a few hours before the worst night of their lives. Then the prayer widens.
He looks past the room, past that night, past the century, and prays for people not yet born. Christians hear themselves in this line.
If you've ever been in a church, a choir, a Bible study, anywhere people pray in his name, this is the moment Christians say he prayed for you.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word; That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me."
Look at the shape of that. The model for oneness is not an organization.

teach.h: ONE, AS THE FATHER AND SON ARE ONE.
teach.b: It's the bond between the Father and the Son: you in me, and I in you. And the purpose points outward: that the world may believe. How Christians treat each other is meant to say something to everyone watching.
Now the honest part. Christians have not always lived this prayer. Churches of the East and West parted ways.
Today there are a great many separate church bodies, and Christians in many of them name that as a real grief. But this verse has also been a seed.
In more recent times, churches long apart began talking, praying together, and in some cases reuniting. That movement is often called ecumenism.

teach.h: UT UNUM SINT: A SEED FOR UNITY.
teach.b: When Pope John Paul the Second wrote a letter on Christian unity in 1995, he titled it with this verse in Latin: Ut unum sint, that they may be one. Protestant and Orthodox voices for unity quote it too.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: Churches still differ, honestly, on what that unity should look like: one visible church, many churches recognizing each other, or a shared life in the Spirit across different names.
The prayer itself doesn't spell it out.

how: Churches in many places keep a yearly Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, often in January, when Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians pray together, often using the words of John 17:21.

practice: Bring to mind a church that isn't yours, or isn't the kind you know best: a cathedral, a storefront chapel, an Orthodox church with icons, a house church, a church in another country.

Picture the people there this week, singing, arguing about the budget, bringing casseroles. If you pray, say his words for them and for your own, that they all may be one; if not, hold them in goodwill for a few breaths.
